Tapri Mart: The Walking Skeleton for Diwali Gifting

1. The scene

It was 7:40 p.m. on Tuesday, 8 September 2026, and the fourth-floor war room of Tapri Mart's office on 100 Feet Road, Indiranagar, still smelled of the filter coffee someone had ordered three hours earlier. Ananya Deshmukh, Group Product Manager for the six-month-old Tapri Gifting line, stood at the whiteboard with a marker that had almost run dry. On the glass wall behind her, a countdown sticky note read "Diwali launch: 41 days." Engineering's next two-week sprint would start at 9 a.m. the following morning, and whatever scope Ananya locked before she left the building tonight was what the team of fourteen engineers would build. There would not be a second sprint before the festival window opened. Her laptop showed three open documents: a backlog of forty-one candidate user stories, a term sheet from a Dubai-based corporate client waiting on a reply, and an email from her own VP asking, simply, "what are we shipping and why."

2. Company background

Tapri Mart had been founded in 2019 by three engineers out of IIT Bombay who promised fifteen-minute grocery delivery from dense clusters of dark stores, the same category that Blinkit, Zepto and Swiggy Instamart were fighting over street by street in Bengaluru, Mumbai, Pune and Hyderabad. By 2026 Tapri Mart operated in forty-two cities, carried an annualised revenue near ₹950 crore, and had learned, like its rivals, that grocery alone carried thin single-digit margins. Blinkit had widened into electronics and pharmacy; Zepto had opened Zepto Café for quick snacks; Tapri Mart's answer, launched that March, was Tapri Gifting — curated hampers of sweets, dry fruits, diyas, and small-batch apparel sourced from Indian MSMEs, promised within three hours of ordering, positioned against slower incumbents such as IGP.com and Ferns N Petals and against Nykaa's seasonal gift sets. Tapri Gifting had done well through the 2026 wedding season, mostly one buyer ordering one hamper for one address, paid by UPI or a saved card through Razorpay, GST invoice generated automatically for the rare business buyer. It had never yet handled an order at the scale, or the complexity, that was now sitting in Ananya's inbox.

3. The situation

Michael Alvarez, Tapri Mart's Sales Head working out of New Jersey to cover the company's growing NRI and Gulf-corporate pipeline, had spent August courting Farasha Retail FZE, a Dubai trading house with roughly six hundred India-based employees spread across Mumbai, Pune and Chennai. Farasha's HR head wanted to buy Diwali hampers centrally from Dubai — one purchase order, one GST-compliant invoice — but have each hamper personalised with the employee's name and delivered to six hundred different home addresses. It was Tapri Mart's first large business-to-business gifting deal, worth ₹85 lakh, and Michael argued it was the door to eleven more corporate leads worth roughly ₹4 crore behind it. Farah Hassan, the Singapore-based customer success lead who would have to service Farasha after signing, was less certain: she had seen enterprise "soft commitments" evaporate when the product could not do what sales had promised.

The consumer side had its own momentum. Priya Chandran, the data scientist working from Toronto, had modelled Diwali-week demand off wedding-season conversion curves and projected close to forty thousand retail gifting orders in the festival week alone — see Exhibit 3 — and argued that a recommendation layer would lift average order value more than any single feature the team could build. Rohit Iyer, the Bengaluru-based engineering lead, had costed the backlog: a full personalisation engine was a ten-week build; a self-serve bulk-order portal with multi-address upload was six weeks; a thin path letting one buyer place a multi-address order manually, routed to ops for confirmation calls, could be live in two to three weeks. Lukas Hoffmann, the lead product designer in Berlin, worried a manual, ops-assisted detour would look amateurish against the polished single-hamper flow the brand had spent six months building.

Ananya's problem was not a shortage of good ideas. Four capable colleagues, each viewing the same forty-one-day deadline from a different city and a different part of the funnel, had each built a case for spending the entire sprint on their own slice of the journey. None of their proposals, alone, got a paying customer — retail or corporate — from discovering a hamper to a delivered gift before Diwali.

Read as a flat, RICE-ranked list, Exhibit 1 argues for building the single-hamper checkout and the recommendation carousel first, since they score highest or touch the largest reach, and for pushing the bulk-order stories to the bottom, since six hundred weekly users looks tiny next to forty thousand. That is exactly the reading Rohit warned against: the scores mix an engineer's effort estimate with a designer's impact guess and a salesperson's confidence number, none calibrated to each other, and none of them says whether a customer can complete an entire journey. A backlog ranked this way can starve a ten-week-old business relationship worth ₹85 lakh while over-investing in a recommendation model nobody has validated.

Exhibit 2 arranges the same stories from Exhibit 1 along the customer's journey rather than by score. The shaded top row is the walking skeleton Ananya is weighing for Release 1; the lower rows are deepening work deferred until usage data exists.

4. The people

Ananya Deshmukh — Group Product Manager, Bengaluru
Owns the release-scope decision and must defend it to her VP by morning; wants a launch that serves both a paying corporate client and organic Diwali demand without betting the whole sprint on either.
Rohit Iyer — Engineering Lead, Bengaluru
Has costed every story in Exhibit 1; wants a scope the team can actually finish in forty-one days, and is wary of promises made in sales calls he did not sit in on.
Priya Chandran — Data Scientist, Toronto
Believes the recommendation engine is the highest-leverage build for retail average order value, and worries that a "thin" launch throws away the wedding-season data she has already modelled.
Lukas Hoffmann — Lead Product Designer, Berlin
Protects the brand's polish; fears an ops-assisted, manual bulk-order path will read as broken next to the retail app's smooth single-hamper flow.
Michael Alvarez — Sales Head, New Jersey
Has verbally committed Farasha Retail FZE to a Diwali delivery date and wants engineering fully behind the corporate bulk-order flow to protect the ₹85 lakh deal and the pipeline behind it.

*Projected retail gifting GMV for Diwali week, based on Priya Chandran's 40,000-order model at an average order value of ₹525, is roughly ₹2.1 crore; the figure shown is the share of that demand estimated to go unserved if no consumer gifting flow is live by the festival, since Tapri Mart's main app would show only groceries. All three paths carry the same fixed engineering headcount of fourteen for the sprint; none assumes additional hiring.

Exhibit 3 makes the trade-off concrete. Building deep on personalisation first (Option A) protects nothing that is contractually due in forty-one days and puts the entire Farasha relationship at risk while also missing the festival window for the feature it was meant to improve. Building only the corporate flow (Option B) secures Farasha but leaves the main consumer opportunity — an order of magnitude larger in weekly volume — sitting behind a grocery-only home screen through the one week of the year gifting demand peaks. Neither path reaches every step of the journey for every customer; both leave a segment with no path at all.

5. The options

Option A — Deepen retail first. Give Priya's ten-week recommendation engine the sprint, betting a smarter, higher-converting retail experience compounds faster than one festival's revenue. The upside is a durable data asset. The cost is definite: the engine will not ship before the festival, Farasha's order likely goes unserved, and Michael's pipeline reads Tapri Mart as unable to execute on its first enterprise deal.

Option B — Win the corporate deal. Put all fourteen engineers on the self-serve bulk-order portal Michael and Farah need for Farasha, finishing in six weeks — just inside the window. The upside is a signed ₹85 lakh account and proof Tapri Mart can serve enterprise buyers. The cost is that retail gifting stays exactly as it is through Diwali week — no curated collections, no gift notes, nothing that turns a grocery visitor into a gifting buyer — forfeiting the far larger consumer opportunity in Exhibit 3.

Option C — Ship the walking skeleton. Build the thinnest version of every step for both segments — a curated collections page, a basic gift note, a single-hamper cart and checkout for retail; an ops-assisted intake call and a manually issued GST invoice for Farasha's six hundred hampers — and defer the recommendation engine, self-serve CSV upload, and live tracking map to a second release once real orders exist. The upside is a working end-to-end path for both segments before Diwali, with Release 2 prioritised from usage rather than guesses. The cost is an unglamorous launch: Farasha's order is confirmed by phone, and Farah's small Singapore team must staff those calls by hand for one festival week.

6. Questions for discussion

  1. Trace the Diwali gifting journey separately for a retail customer and for Farasha's HR buyer. At which steps do the two journeys share the same backbone, and where do they genuinely need different stories?
  2. Using Exhibit 1, which stories belong in a walking skeleton and which are "deepening" work that can wait? Why does ranking the same backlog by RICE alone point Ananya toward a different, weaker scope?
  3. What does Exhibit 3 imply about the true cost of Options A and B once both segments' demand is considered together, rather than one team's slice in isolation?
  4. If Ananya chooses Option C, what should she watch for in the first two weeks of live orders to decide whether Release 2 should deepen personalisation (Priya's case) or self-serve bulk tooling (Michael's case)?

7. A note for the learner

User story mapping exists for exactly the trap Ananya is in. A flat, scored backlog like Exhibit 1 tells you what one team member believes is valuable in isolation; it says nothing about whether a customer can walk from discovering a hamper to receiving one. Arranging the same stories along the customer's journey, as in Exhibit 2, turns the question from "what scores highest" into "what is the thinnest slice that crosses every step, for the customers who must transact this week." That thinnest end-to-end slice — the walking skeleton — is deliberately shallow everywhere and complete nowhere in particular, which is uncomfortable for specialists like Priya and Lukas, each wanting to go deep on their own step first.

A well-reasoned answer does three things. First, it builds one backbone that both retail and corporate customers can walk, substituting a manual or "ops-assisted" story wherever full automation cannot be ready in time, rather than skipping a step for one segment entirely — an intake call and a manually issued invoice are still stories on the map, not shortcuts around it. Second, it explicitly defers the stories that make any one step excellent — the recommendation engine, the self-serve bulk upload, the tracking map — to a release informed by real usage rather than by whoever argued most persuasively on 8 September. Third, it treats each stakeholder's discomfort as information about risk to monitor, not as a veto.

On that basis, Option C is the defensible path. It is the only option under which both the ₹85 lakh Farasha relationship and the far larger retail Diwali window are live, even imperfectly, when the festival arrives — Exhibit 3 shows Options A and B each forfeit one side of that trade entirely, while Option C forfeits neither. The reasoning is not that manual, ops-assisted processes are the goal; they are an honest, temporary story on the map, sized to the six hundred orders that need them this year, bought at three weeks instead of the ten to fourteen that automating either side alone would take. Ananya's task the next morning is not to announce a perfect product; it is to set a firm two-week checkpoint, once real retail and Farasha orders have moved through the skeleton, at which Priya's and Michael's competing cases for Release 2 are settled by data rather than by who spoke last in the war room.

Rahdaari Finserv: The Loan That Never Reaches the Road

A case prepared for classroom discussion. Rahdaari Finserv, Mizan Fleet Finance, Sarhad Roadlines and Chaupal Small Finance Bank are fictional composites; regulators, public infrastructure and named competitors are real.

1. Kalyani Nagar, 11:40 p.m.

On the night of Sunday, 29 November 2026, rain was coming off the Mula-Mutha in sheets and Meera Raghunathan had two laptops open on her dining table in Kalyani Nagar, Pune. On the left was the board deck due at 8 a.m.; on the right, a spreadsheet of sixty-three user stories that the product, engineering and risk teams had been arguing over since the October offsite in Lonavala. Between the two laptops lay a printout she had annotated in three colours and then given up on.

At 9:30 the next morning, Rahdaari Finserv's board would ask Meera, Director of Product, one question in three different forms: what will the eleven hundred engineer-weeks available between now and the end of March buy, and when does the digital lending channel stop being a pilot. Arvind Joshi, the co-founder and chief executive, had put it more plainly on Friday in the corridor outside the Baner office: "One roadmap, one number. I don't want four teams each explaining why their part is the important part."

Two messages had arrived in the previous hour. The first was a WhatsApp voice note from Ramesh Waghmare in Nagpur, timestamped 10:52 p.m., about a file for a two-truck owner in Wardha, sanctioned eleven days earlier, with still no money in the seller's account. The second was an email from Vikram Sethi in New Jersey, subject line "Mizan parity clause — need a position before Gulf Monday," and one line of body text: "Meera, I can hold them for a week. Not two."

What made the night difficult was not that Meera lacked options. It was that she had four, each defended by a competent colleague with real evidence, and that the numbers those colleagues cited did not agree with one another.

2. How Rahdaari came to be shaped this way

Rahdaari Finserv Technologies was founded in Pune in 2019 by Arvind Joshi, who had spent fourteen years in used commercial vehicle collections at a large southern NBFC, and Sudhanshu Katti, an engineer from an IT services background in Bengaluru. Their first product was unglamorous: a loan origination system sold to regional non-banking finance companies lending against second-hand trucks — the Tata Ace and Ashok Leyland Dost class at the small end, ten-to-sixteen-tonne haulage at the large end. By 2022 twenty-three NBFCs used the software. In August of that year Rahdaari bought a dormant Maharashtra-registered NBFC for ₹38 crore and began lending off its own balance sheet, which turned a software company into a regulated lender with a risk committee and a compliance officer.

Two decisions from that period still shape what Rahdaari can do. The first was architectural. In 2021, to win a large NBFC client, the origination engine was built around a mandatory physical inspection: a field officer visits, photographs the chassis number, checks the registration certificate against the seller's papers, enters a valuation. That assumption is hard-wired into roughly forty screens and into the sanction state machine itself; no loan can be approved without a field officer's identifier on the file.

The second was commercial. In March 2024, with a ₹240 crore Series C closing and a Gulf licensing deal on the table, Rahdaari had ninety days to demonstrate its stack to Mizan Fleet Finance, a Dubai lender financing fleet operators across the UAE and Oman. Building a properly multi-tenant, configurable core would have taken nine months. Sudhanshu forked the codebase instead, promising the merge would happen "next quarter." Nineteen months later the fork still exists. Every change to the India journey must be decided again for the Gulf build, and Exhibit 6 shows what that costs.

Figure 1. The two business models overlap from 2022; the forked Gulf build runs alongside the India platform from March 2024. Dates from the October 2026 investor update.

3. The industry around the decision

Used commercial vehicle finance in India is a large, old and stubbornly manual business. Shriram Finance, Cholamandalam, Mahindra Finance, Sundaram Finance and Tata Motors Finance built it over decades on branch networks and field relationships, lending to borrowers whose income arrives in cash and whose documentation is thin. Bajaj Finance and a wave of fintech lenders squeezed in through adjacent, smaller-ticket categories. Rahdaari's wedge was the single-truck and two-truck owner — the driver who has saved for a decade and wants to stop driving someone else's vehicle — a segment the incumbents serve but serve slowly.

The public digital infrastructure has moved faster than the industry's operating model. Aadhaar and CKYC identity checks are routine; the Account Aggregator framework, under Sahamati's operating rules, lets a borrower share bank statements in minutes with consent; the Parivahan and Vahan databases hold registration and hypothecation records; NPCI's e-NACH and UPI Autopay rails collect the instalment. NETC FASTag data from NHAI toll plazas can show how many kilometres a truck actually runs, and GSTN filings show turnover. The Reserve Bank's digital lending directions require a Key Fact Statement in the borrower's language, a cooling-off period, disbursal into the borrower's own bank account rather than a third party's except in defined cases, and a named grievance officer. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 governs consent for every one of those pulls, and default loss guarantees given to sourcing partners are capped.

The effect is that a lender can assemble a borrower's identity, income and collateral in under ten minutes — and still take eleven days to hand over the money, because the last steps run through an RTO counter, a seller's bank account and a mandate registration that fails for anyone banking with a district co-operative society. Rahdaari's exposure also runs outward: Mizan in Dubai, where Emirates ID replaces Aadhaar, there is no Vahan and no e-NACH, and the interface must render right-to-left in Arabic. Harpreet Bhatia in Singapore has two further Gulf prospects, and Vikram has been asked about Kenya.

4. What happened, and what has since turned out to be wrong

In January 2026 the board set a target: ₹900 crore of assets under management by FY28, with at least thirty per cent of originations coming through a direct digital channel, against four per cent at the time. The programme was named Rapid. In March a pilot went live in Nashik and Nagpur with a deliberately hybrid design: a digital front end for discovery, eligibility and document collection, and Ramesh's field officers for everything after sanction.

At the June offsite a consultant introduced RICE scoring. Five story owners scored the backlog over two days. The programme then built, in order, what scored highest: an eligibility checker quoting an indicative EMI in forty seconds, an Account Aggregator bank-statement pull, WhatsApp lead capture, and a Marathi and Hindi interface. By September the numbers in Exhibit 2 were being shown to investors: sixty-one per cent of applicants who began the digital form completed it, and time to sanction fell from four days to under six hours.

Then October's operating review produced Exhibit 3. Of 12,900 leads entering the funnel between March and October, 1,190 files were sanctioned and 340 disbursed. Median time from sanction to money in the seller's account was 11.4 days against a promise of forty-eight hours. Three assumptions had quietly failed. First, e-NACH mandate registration succeeded for only 54 per cent of borrowers, not the 90 per cent assumed, because a large share of small fleet owners bank with district central co-operative banks that are not reachable destinations on the rail; the fallback was a physical mandate posted to Mumbai. Second, hypothecation endorsement on the registration certificate, without which the loan is effectively unsecured, still required a visit to the regional transport office in most of Maharashtra and Madhya Pradesh, and the product had no state for "disbursed but not yet endorsed." Third, Devika Nair's approval model, whose lift had justified loosening the credit policy in July, drew most of its power from a bureau vintage feature — and 38 per cent of the target segment is new to credit, with no bureau file at all.

A fourth discovery was more uncomfortable. When Meera's analyst reconciled Exhibit 2 against the field roster in November, 44 per cent of the "digital" applications turned out to have been keyed in by a field officer sitting next to the borrower. The channel the board believed was self-serve was, for nearly half its volume, Ramesh's team typing faster than the borrower could.

Meanwhile Sarhad Roadlines, a Nagpur fleet operator with 220 trucks that refers its own driver-owners to Rahdaari and accounts for roughly ₹62 crore of annual sourcing, sent a renewal letter on 14 November noting that three of its referrals had waited more than a fortnight. And on 19 November Mizan formally invoked the parity clause in its licence agreement.

Figure 2. Drawn by the product analyst on 24 November 2026 from the origination database and the field roster. The first four steps use a different denominator from the last nine — see the footnote to Exhibit 3.

5. The people

Meera Raghunathan — Director of Product, Pune
Owns the roadmap and the Monday answer. Her quarterly objective is the share of originations coming through the digital channel. She championed the RICE exercise in June and privately believes it produced a roadmap that optimised steps and completed no journey — not something she wants to say for the first time in front of the board.
Sudhanshu Katti — Co-founder and CTO, Bengaluru
Wants the Gulf fork merged before anything else, and argues that every quarter of delay compounds. He is not saying that two of his four senior backend engineers have interviewed elsewhere this month, one with a Chennai SaaS firm at a package the hiring freeze forbids him to match, and that both gave the fork as the reason.
Zoya Qureshi — Chief Risk and Compliance Officer, Mumbai
Signs the compliance attestations personally. Her position is that no regulated step — the Key Fact Statement, the cooling-off period, the endorsement — can be delivered in thin or provisional form, and that a disbursed loan without endorsement is an unsecured loan carried at secured provisioning. A former colleague has told her informally to expect scrutiny in the first quarter; she has not put that in writing.
Devika Nair — Principal Data Scientist, Toronto
Wants six engineers for a quarter to rebuild the approval model on alternate data: FASTag movement, GST filings, route-level freight rates. Her incentive is a model that generalises to new-to-credit borrowers. She has not volunteered that the AUC she reported in July falls materially once bureau-thin borrowers are included, which undermines the credit-policy loosening built on it.
Lea Brandt — Head of Design, Berlin
Spent ten days in Nagpur and Wardha in September and returned with a journey map covering thirteen steps. She argues the team has been designing screens, not a journey. She has also drafted, and not circulated, a version of the flow in which the field officer disappears entirely — a design she knows would read, in Nagpur, as a redundancy plan for 140 people.
Vikram Sethi — SVP, Global Platform Sales, New Jersey
Carries the licence revenue number and is compensated on annual contract value, not on Indian AUM. He wants parity features shipped for Mizan and two further Gulf logos behind them. He has not told the board that Mizan's chief operating officer already offered a ninety-day extension, because he judges that the deadline pressure is the only thing that will move engineering.
Harpreet Bhatia — Director of Customer Success, Singapore
Services Mizan across a two-and-a-half-hour time difference and sits on every escalation. She reports that Mizan's operations team has built local workarounds it is comfortable with, and would privately prefer a configurable core in nine months to a parity release in three. She has not said this to Vikram, whose deal it is.
Ramesh Waghmare — Head of Field Operations, Nagpur
Runs 140 field officers across Vidarbha, Marathwada and eastern Madhya Pradesh at roughly ₹4.9 crore a year, and his budget is defended by volume. His position is that manual steps are the only reason anything gets disbursed. He has not told Pune how much of the digital channel's volume his officers key in themselves.

"Parity is not a feature request, it is a clause. Every week we spend arguing about RTO offices in Madhya Pradesh is a week of a ₹6.5 crore milestone I have to explain in Dubai."

— Vikram Sethi, email to Meera and Arvind, 27 November 2026

"Honest note before Monday: the model that justified the July policy change is weaker than the deck says for anyone without a bureau file. I can fix it. I need six people and a quarter, and I need someone to decide whether we are underwriting trucks or people."

— Devika Nair, message to Meera, 26 November, 9:14 p.m. Toronto time

"Mizan's ops head asked me last week whether they could just keep their workarounds and take a proper configurable version later. I did not know what I was allowed to say."

— Harpreet Bhatia, weekly call notes, 24 November 2026

8. The options as Meera sees them tonight

Option A — finish the funnel. Spend the quarter on the post-sanction steps: the seller payout rail, the RTO endorsement tracker, the e-NACH fallback, borrower servicing and the grievance workflow. Fifty-four engineer-weeks of the 702 available. This closes the gap between Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3 and makes the existing assisted journey work. It does nothing for Mizan, nothing for the fork, and nothing for the digital-share objective on which Meera is measured, since a faster assisted journey is still an assisted journey.

Option B — a narrow fully digital slice. Pick one segment — a single-truck buyer with a bureau file, purchasing from an organised dealer, registering in one of three RTOs where the state has an online endorsement path — and build every step for that borrower with no field officer at all. Perhaps eight per cent of current volume; the digital-share number would still look poor in March, but the company would, for the first time, own a complete path.

Option C — pay the platform debt. Merge the fork, ninety-six weeks, and satisfy Mizan's parity obligation as a by-product rather than as a special build. Sudhanshu's argument is that every India feature currently costs Rahdaari twice, that Exhibit 6's deduction is understated, and that his senior engineers will leave over it. The cost is a quarter in which no borrower's experience improves.

Option D — the growth roadmap. Fund Devika's alternate-data model and the front-end stories that scored highest in Exhibit 1, and keep the back half manual. This is the path of least internal conflict and the one the RICE ranking already endorses.

Meera had written the four options on a sheet under the heading "where do 1,100 weeks go." She had also written, and then scratched out, a note to herself: this is a capacity question only if the journey is a given. All four options assume the journey ends when the money leaves Rahdaari's account. Zoya's point at the risk committee suggests it does not: a loan disbursed without hypothecation endorsement and without a live mandate is neither secured nor collectible, which means the thinnest thing that actually works may run further to the right of Figure 2 than anyone has been budgeting for. It may also run further to the left. Ramesh's officers are not a workaround inside the journey; for 44 per cent of the funnel they are the journey, and no option on the sheet says what they are supposed to do on the day the product works.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The roadmap locks at Monday's 9:30 a.m. board call; sprint planning follows at 2 p.m. in Bengaluru, which is 4:30 a.m. in Toronto and 11 p.m. Sunday in New Jersey, so two of the eight stakeholders will read the outcome rather than attend. Headcount is frozen at 61 engineers until the Series D closes; Arvind has told only Meera that a term sheet conversation is live and that the investor asked specifically about the Gulf revenue line. Series C runway ends in February 2028 at current burn. The Mizan milestone falls on 31 January 2027, carrying a ₹4.2 crore penalty and a termination right. The co-lending arrangement with Chaupal Small Finance Bank, which funds 62 per cent of disbursals, requires monthly portfolio-quality reporting, and the default loss guarantee is capped by regulation, so deteriorating collections cannot be absorbed by widening it. The Sarhad Roadlines sourcing agreement renews on 15 December. Digital lending compliance changes must be in production by 31 March 2027. Ramesh's 140 officers cost ₹4.9 crore a year and are on rolls, not contract.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. Lay Exhibits 2 and 3 side by side. What is each one measuring, and what would you have to know before you could tell the board which of the two describes the business?
  2. Exhibit 1 ranks the grievance workflow second from last and the fork merge last. What is it about the way the backlog was constructed and scored that produces this result, and what would change if the same sixty-three stories were arranged differently?
  3. Using Figure 2, define what "working" means for a single-truck owner in Wardha. At which step is the loan first useful to him, and at which step is it first safe for Rahdaari? What follows if those two steps are not the same?
  4. Exhibit 4 suggests an assisted file costs almost twice a digital one. Given the footnote, how much weight should Meera put on that comparison, and what would you measure instead before reducing Ramesh's headcount?
  5. Vikram has not disclosed Mizan's offer of an extension; Harpreet believes Mizan would prefer a configurable core later. Whose information should govern the Gulf decision, and how should Meera obtain it without making an enemy of the person who owns the account?
  6. It is 8 a.m. on Monday. What does Meera put in the deck, what does she tell the board about the September numbers they have already seen, and what does she ask the board to decide rather than decide herself?

11. After midnight

By 1:40 a.m. the rain had stopped. Meera had drawn the thirteen steps of Figure 2 across the back of the printout and begun writing story titles under each, then stopped, because under three of the steps she could not name a single story anyone had written. She thought about the seller in Wardha who had waited eleven days and had a buyer offering cash; about Zoya's flat sentence at the risk committee and Harpreet's careful one; about the number on slide four, sixty-one per cent, which was true and which she now understood to mean almost nothing.

Her laptop showed 1,098 engineer-weeks and four options and no way to fit them together that did not disappoint at least three of the people whose evidence she had been reading all night. She closed the spreadsheet, opened a blank page, and typed a heading she was not yet sure she could defend: What has to be true for one borrower to finish. Then she sat looking at it while the first buses started up on the Nagar Road.

User Story Mapping

Arranging work along the journey in order to find the thinnest end-to-end slice that still works — Delivery & Technology › Prioritisation & Decision-Making.

1. Eleven weeks, two hundred and forty stories

On the morning of 4 March 2024, Ananya Bhide sat in a glass-walled room on the third floor of Rudrani Bazaar's office in Baner, Pune, looking at a spreadsheet with 240 rows in it. Rudrani Bazaar was a four-year-old marketplace for pre-owned two-wheelers: buyers browsed scooters and motorcycles, sellers listed them, and the company took a fee on each completed transfer. Bhide, who had joined eighteen months earlier from a payments company, was the head of product for the seller side. The 240 rows were the engineering team's estimate of everything that would have to exist for a new proposition the founders had approved in January and called, internally, Instant Sale.

The promise of Instant Sale was simple enough to fit on a billboard: a seller would describe their bike, receive a guaranteed price within two minutes, have the bike inspected at home, and be paid the same day. The promise was also, as Bhide's tech lead Faizan Qureshi kept pointing out, an end-to-end promise. There was no useful halfway house. A seller who received a price but could not book an inspection had received nothing. A seller who was inspected but not paid had been actively harmed.

The arithmetic was unforgiving. Nine engineers, eleven weeks to the start of the festive selling season, roughly fifty-five working days each. That was 495 engineer-days, and the team's own history said about a fifth of that would disappear into production defects, support escalations and the interruptions of a live marketplace. Call it 396 days of real capacity. The 240 rows added up to an estimate of 1,140 days. Instant Sale, as specified, was roughly three times too large, and the festive window would not move.

The obvious response — the one Bhide had seen fail twice in her career — was to sort the 240 rows by a priority score and draw a line at row 90. The trouble is that a backlog sorted by score has no memory of the journey it came from. The top ninety rows in Rudrani Bazaar's spreadsheet included eleven stories about photo quality guidance and not one about transferring money. Scored individually, each of those eleven was defensible. Assembled, they were not a product. What Bhide needed was not a better score. It was a different shape of the same information.

2. The idea, stated precisely

A user story map is a two-dimensional arrangement of planned work in which the horizontal axis is the user's journey through the product in the order they experience it, and the vertical axis is depth of elaboration within each step of that journey. Along the top runs a row of user activities — the large things a person is trying to accomplish, read left to right as a narrative — which practitioners call the backbone. Beneath each activity sit the specific steps the user takes, and beneath each step sit the individual user stories: small, independently describable pieces of functionality, conventionally written in the form "as a seller I want to upload a photograph of the chassis number so that the inspector can verify it in advance."

The point of the second dimension is that it lets you cut horizontally. A horizontal line drawn across the whole map, taking the top one or two stories from every column, defines a release: a set of work that is thin in every activity but complete across all of them. The thinnest such line that still produces a working, usable, end-to-end product is what Alistair Cockburn named a walking skeleton — a tiny implementation of the system that performs a small end-to-end function, with the real architecture and the real integrations in place, however crudely. It walks. It is a skeleton. Both halves of the phrase are load-bearing.

The technique was developed by Jeff Patton, an American product-design consultant, who first wrote it up around 2005 in an article whose title is the entire argument — It's All in How You Slice It — and expanded it into a book in 2014. The problem it was invented to solve was specific and, by then, well documented. Agile methods had replaced the large requirements document with the flat backlog: a single ranked list of stories. The flat list solved a real problem (nobody read the document) and created a new one (nobody could see the whole). Teams lost the ability to answer two questions that the old document, for all its faults, had answered easily: what is the shape of the thing we are building, and what is missing?

The sentence Bhide could say in a meeting without sounding glib: "Before we decide what to cut, let's lay the work out along the seller's journey, because I want the first release to be thin everywhere rather than finished in a few places and absent in others."

3. How it actually works

The mechanics have six steps, and practitioners routinely leave the second and the fifth implicit, which is where most of the damage is done.

First, choose the user and the journey. A map is always a map of one person's path. Rudrani Bazaar has sellers, buyers, inspectors, and the ops executives who call sellers; four different maps. Bhide's team drew the seller map because Instant Sale was a seller proposition, and drew a small separate map for the inspector because the inspector's steps had their own dependencies. Mixing two users in one backbone is the single most common structural error, because the resulting row cannot be released: it is half of one person's experience and half of another's.

Second — the implicit step — write the backbone from observed behaviour, not from the product's screens. The temptation is to name the activities after the screens you already intend to build. Bhide's team instead used the customer journey map the research team had produced in November, which was built from twenty-two seller interviews and had already established that sellers experienced "waiting to find out if the price holds" as a distinct and anxious phase. That phase had no screen. It became activity 6, Accept final offer, and it turned out to carry the riskiest work on the map. A backbone derived from screens would never have contained it.

Third, decompose each activity into steps, then each step into stories. This is ordinary backlog work; the map adds only the constraint that every story must live under exactly one step, and every step under exactly one activity. Stories that refuse to sit anywhere are informative: they are usually infrastructure ("upgrade the payments SDK") or they belong to a different user's map.

Fourth, order each column by necessity, not by value. Within a column, the top card is the crudest version of the step that still lets the user continue. In column 4, Book the inspection, the top card was not a slot picker; it was "ops executive telephones the seller and writes the slot into the admin panel." That is not a good experience. It is a step that works.

Fifth — the other implicit step — name the riskiest assumption before you draw the release line. A map does not, by itself, tell you where to cut. It gives you a menu of legitimate cuts. The cut you choose depends on what you are trying to learn. We will see in the next section that two entirely different skeletons of almost identical cost fall out of two different answers to the question "what would sink this if we were wrong about it?"

Sixth, draw the line and test it by walking it. Read the cards above the line aloud, left to right, as a story about one named seller on one named Tuesday. If the narration ever requires a sentence beginning "and then somehow", the line is wrong.

4. The worked example, with the arithmetic shown

On 6 March, Bhide's team laid the 240 stories onto the backbone and then, column by column, asked a single question: what is the crudest card in this column that still lets a real seller continue to the next column? The result is the left-hand half of Table 1.

Two numbers in that table deserve attention. The first is 154 against 396: the skeleton consumes 39% of available capacity, which is the right order of magnitude. A skeleton that eats 90% of the budget is not a skeleton; it is the plan with a thin coat of humility. The second is column 7, where the skeleton keeps 34 of 221 days — by far the largest absolute retention. That is deliberate. Money must be real from the first release. A seller who is told the payout worked when it did not has been defrauded, not experimented on, and no amount of learning justifies it.

The second pass: one input changes

On 11 March, the team ran a pre-mortem. Qureshi asked the question that the fifth, implicit step of the method requires: if Instant Sale fails in October, what will have been the reason? The room did not say "we could not build the pricing service." It said, almost unanimously, that sellers would not accept an algorithmically generated price without a human to argue with, and would walk to the neighbourhood dealer who offered ₹3,000 more in cash. Rudrani Bazaar's own data supported the worry: in the existing classifieds product, 61% of completed sales involved at least one price negotiation message.

That single change of belief — from "the risk is building it" to "the risk is them accepting the price" — redrew the line. The team went back to the map and re-cut it, keeping the budget roughly constant.

This is the part of the method that is easy to miss and hard to unlearn once seen. The map did not change the budget: 154 days became 164, a rounding error at this scale. What changed was where the budget went, and therefore what the team would know in eleven weeks. Plan A would have proven that Rudrani Bazaar could build an instant-sale pipeline. Plan B would prove whether sellers in Pune would accept one. Only the second was in doubt.

Notice also what the map made visible that a scored list would have hidden. In the flat backlog, the three counter-offer stories sat at ranks 96, 141 and 203, because individually each looked like a refinement. Sitting in column 6, directly under the activity the pre-mortem had named as fatal, their rank was obviously wrong. The map did not compute a better priority. It put the stories in a place where a human could see that the priority was wrong.

5. Nuances a learner must become aware of

A map is a map of one user, and the choice of user is the first real decision

Every column boundary on a backbone is an assertion about how one specific person experiences time. Change the person and the backbone changes entirely: Rudrani Bazaar's inspector experiences "reach the address, assess, submit" where the seller experiences "wait, worry, accept." Teams that draw one map for "the user" produce a backbone that belongs to nobody, and then cannot explain why the release line keeps leaving holes. If two users must both be served for the product to work at all — which is the normal condition in marketplaces — draw both maps and align them on the shared events, rather than merging them into one row.

The backbone is narrative order, not dependency order and not priority order

The horizontal axis is the sequence in which the user lives through the product. It is not a project plan. Column 7 is not built last; in Bhide's case it was started first, because the payout integration with the bank's IMPS channel had a four-week lead time. Confusing narrative order with build order is the most common misreading among people who have seen a story map once, and it produces plans where the team spends five weeks polishing the first two columns because those are "first."

"Thin" means crude, not partial

The top card in a column must be a complete step done badly, never a good step done halfway. "Ops executive telephones the seller" is thin and complete. "Slot picker that works only for Pune 411045" is thin and partial, and it produces a release that walks for some sellers and collapses for others, which teaches you nothing because you cannot tell whether the sellers who dropped out were rejecting the proposition or hitting the gap.

Manual is a legitimate implementation of a step

Nothing in the method requires that a card be built in software. A step performed by a person with a spreadsheet satisfies the walking-skeleton condition, provided the user's experience of that step is real. This is why column 5 in plan B costs four engineer-days: the inspection genuinely happens, the seller genuinely experiences it, and only the automation is deferred. The discipline is to be honest about the operating cost and to set in advance the volume at which the manual step must be replaced.

The map does not tell you where to cut; your riskiest assumption does

This is the nuance that separates practitioners from vocabulary users. A map is a structured menu of feasible releases. Choosing among them requires a belief about what is uncertain, and that belief comes from research, from a pre-mortem, from support tickets — from outside the map. A team that draws a beautiful map and then cuts "evenly" has automated a judgement that should have been made consciously. Ask any team showing you a story map: which card on this map are you least sure about, and does the line you have drawn put it above or below?

Estimates on a map are still estimates, and they are systematically wrong in a particular direction

Bhide's 1,140 days carried no confidence interval. Story-level estimates are biased low for exactly the work the map makes thin, because the crude version of a step often has to handle the same edge cases as the elaborate one — a payout of ₹47,000 and a payout of ₹1,40,000 both have to clear bank verification even if the interface is ugly. Treat the skeleton's estimate as the number most likely to be exceeded, and size the first slice to leave slack rather than to consume the budget.

A story map does not price anything, and cannot replace a scoring method

The map answers "what must be in the release for it to work?" It is silent on "which of these two equally releasable slices is worth more?" That second question is what value-versus-effort, RICE and weighted scoring exist for. The relationship is layered, not competitive: the map defines the set of admissible slices; a scoring method chooses among them. Running RICE over a flat list without a map produces scores for items that cannot ship together — the failure the module's benchmark is warning about when it cautions against teaching RICE as vocabulary. A high-scoring story that leaves an empty column is worth nothing until the column is filled.

What the technique cannot tell you, however well applied

It cannot tell you whether the journey itself is the right journey. Rudrani Bazaar's map assumes sellers want a guaranteed instant price. If sellers actually want a higher price and are willing to wait three weeks, the map is a well-organised plan for building the wrong product, and no amount of slicing will reveal it — the skeleton will walk, competently, in the wrong direction. The map is downstream of the proposition. It disciplines execution; it does not validate strategy. That is why it sits directly downstream of customer journey mapping in this curriculum, and why a map drawn without research is drawn on sand.

6. How this differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the backbone is usually short, well understood and easily observed, and the hard work is vertical: there are forty defensible ways to implement "describe the bike" and the map's value is in forcing a choice of the crudest one. A consumer learning app such as Rudravan Learning can put a genuinely thin slice in front of ten thousand users in a week and read the answer from behaviour.

In B2B and enterprise products the backbone is longer, less visible and frequently spans several people inside the customer. At Rudrayan Instruments, which sells diagnostic equipment software to pathology laboratories, the journey for a single test result passes through a technician, a pathologist and a billing clerk, and the walking skeleton must therefore cross three users to be a skeleton at all. The second complication is that enterprise buyers often cannot accept a crude step: a laboratory cannot use a manual workaround for a step that a National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories audit will examine. In such cases thinness must be achieved by narrowing the population — one laboratory, one test type — rather than by crudeness.

In marketplaces, of which Rudrani Bazaar is one, the map has a structural peculiarity: two backbones must be walked simultaneously or neither walks. A seller journey that completes requires a buyer journey that completes, and the first release must contain a thin version of both, or the company must manually supply the missing side. Bhide's plan B does exactly this — Rudrani Bazaar itself buys the bike, so the buyer journey is deferred entirely. That is a legitimate skeleton, but it converts the company into the counterparty and puts working capital at risk, which is a decision for the CFO and not for the product team alone.

By stage, the difference is less about the technique and more about who is in the room. In a twenty-person company the map is usually drawn in an afternoon by everyone who will build it, and its main value is shared understanding. In a two-thousand-person company the same map crosses three teams with three roadmaps, and its main value becomes negotiation: the map is the artefact on which the payments team and the seller team can see that their release lines must be the same line. Large organisations also tend to draw maps and then ignore the release lines under quarterly planning pressure, which is why a map in a large company needs a named owner who is accountable for the line, not just for the cards.

7. Common mistakes and the cheapest diagnostic for each

The layer-cake release

Symptom from outside: a status report saying the team is 60% complete in week eight, with nothing a user can do. Underlying misunderstanding: that "complete" refers to components rather than to journeys. Cheapest diagnostic: ask what a named user could accomplish today, end to end. If the answer requires the word "once", the release is horizontal.

The map that is really a sitemap

Symptom: the backbone reads "Home, Search, Listing, Checkout, Account" — the names of screens. Misunderstanding: that the journey is what the product does rather than what the person does. Diagnostic: read the backbone aloud with the subject "the seller" in front of each box. "The seller Account" is not a sentence, and the failure is immediately audible.

The line that is drawn by capacity rather than by risk

Symptom: the first release contains precisely the number of stories that fits the sprint, and the team cannot say what it expects to learn. Misunderstanding: that slicing is an exercise in fitting rather than in choosing. Diagnostic: ask what result from release one would cause the plan for release two to change. Silence means the slice was chosen by arithmetic.

The map drawn once and never touched

Symptom: a photograph of sticky notes in a Confluence page dated four months ago while the team works from a Jira board that no longer resembles it. Misunderstanding: that the map is a planning ceremony rather than a living representation of the plan. Diagnostic: ask where a story added yesterday lives on the map. If nobody can point to the column, the map has died and the flat list has quietly reasserted itself.

8. What good looks like

A team that has internalised this behaves visibly differently in a planning meeting. When a senior stakeholder asks for a feature, they do not say yes or no; they ask which column it sits in and which card it sits above. When the deadline compresses, they do not remove the last three items from a ranked list — they raise the release line evenly and then ask which two columns must stay thick because that is where the uncertainty lives. Their release notes read like a sentence about a person rather than an inventory of components. And when the first release ships, they can state in advance, on paper, the specific number that will tell them whether the assumption held: in Bhide's case, the proportion of sellers receiving an algorithmic price who accept it without a counter-offer, with 45% set as the threshold below which the proposition would be reconsidered.

9. What Ananya Bhide decided

On 14 March, Bhide took plan B to the founders with three slides: the map, Table 2, and a single line of reasoning. Instant Sale's engineering risk was ordinary and its commercial risk was not, so the first eleven weeks would spend 58 of 164 engineer-days on the pricing and offer experience, run inspections manually with three contract inspectors at roughly ₹1.9 lakh a month, and launch to one postal-code cluster in west Pune on 27 May. The buyer side would not be built; Rudrani Bazaar would take the bikes onto its own book, capped at ₹40 lakh of working capital, which the CFO agreed to as an explicit and bounded experiment. The measure was acceptance rate, and the decision point was 15 July.

What to learn next follows directly from what the map cannot do. The map produces a set of admissible slices; choosing between two slices that both walk requires a way to compare value against effort, which is where value-versus-effort matrices and then RICE scoring enter — and those techniques are only safe once you can already tell whether a candidate slice leaves a hole. Beneath both sits customer journey mapping, which is where a trustworthy backbone comes from in the first place.

Two questions to sit with. First: on the last plan you were part of, could a named user have completed a whole task at the end of the first release — and if not, what did the team believe it had learned at that point? Second: when you next see a team cut scope, watch whether they cut the bottom off a list or raise a line across a journey, and ask which of the two the situation actually called for.
