A full treatment: how arranging work along the journey converts prioritisation from ranking into a constrained choice — and what the technique still refuses to tell you. Delivery & Technology › Prioritisation & Decision-Making.

1. Two rooms, two deadlines

At 8.40 on the morning of 11 September 2025, Devika Raman stood in front of a wall in Rudraksh Grid Systems' office off Bannerghatta Road in Bengaluru, on which four squads had spent two days laying out 612 index cards. Rudraksh Grid Systems sold meter-data management and consumer-billing software to state electricity distribution companies. In July it had signed a ₹9.4 crore contract to go live with 4 lakh smart-metered consumers by 1 April 2026, in a rollout funded under the national distribution-sector scheme, with liquidated damages of ₹1.1 crore attaching to a slip beyond thirty days. The 612 cards represented 5,400 engineer-days of estimated work. Raman had thirty-four engineers and twenty-six weeks, which after leave, incident load and the two engineers permanently on the previous customer's escalations came to about 3,060 days. She was short by a factor of 1.8.

Nine hundred kilometres away in Lower Parel, Mumbai, on the afternoon of 15 September, Nikhil Barve had a smaller version of the same wall and a sharper version of the same problem. Barve was group product manager at Rohanika Money, a four-year-old consumer savings and investment app with 2.8 million registered users, of whom 410,000 had ever transacted. The company's board had approved a goal-based investing proposition — name a goal, receive a plan, invest monthly towards it — and had set an internal launch date of 1 December to catch the January salary-hike season. Barve had thirteen engineers, ten weeks, roughly 507 usable engineer-days, and a backlog of 287 stories estimated at 1,460 days. He was short by a factor of 2.9.

Both had been given the same well-meaning advice by the same kind of person: rank the backlog and draw a line. Both had reasons to distrust it. Raman's reason was structural — a billing system that generates a bill but cannot deliver it to a consumer is not 80% of a billing system, it is zero billing systems. Barve's reason was historical: eighteen months earlier Rohanika Money had shipped a ranked-list release of a tax-saving product in which everything above the line worked beautifully and the last step, redemption, was scheduled for the following quarter. Support absorbed 3,100 tickets in six weeks and the feature was withdrawn.

This page is about the technique both of them reached for, and about the thing that technique does and does not do. The argument it will build is this: a story map's real output is not a plan. It is a constraint set. It converts prioritisation from "rank these 612 items" into a different and much better-posed problem — "choose at least one card from each of nine columns, subject to a budget of 3,060 days" — and in doing so it exposes a residual decision that the method itself is silent about, namely what to do with the slack once the minimum feasible skeleton is paid for. Everything interesting about expertise in this area lives in that residual.

2. The idea, its history, and the schools that disagree about it

A user story map is a two-dimensional arrangement of planned work. The horizontal axis is one user's journey through the product in the order they live it; the row of large activities along the top is called the backbone. The vertical axis under each activity is elaboration: the steps within that activity, and beneath them individual user stories — small units of functionality expressible as something a named person can do. Because the vertical axis is elaboration rather than sequence, a horizontal line drawn across the whole map defines a candidate release that is thin in every activity and absent in none. The thinnest such line that still produces something a user can complete end to end is a walking skeleton, a term Alistair Cockburn introduced for a tiny implementation that exercises the real architecture end to end while doing almost nothing well.

The technique was articulated by Jeff Patton, working as a product-design consultant in the mid-2000s, in an article whose title carries the whole thesis — It's All in How You Slice It, around 2005 — and expanded in his 2014 book. Its intellectual parentage is specific. From extreme programming it inherited the story as the unit of work and the flat product backlog as the container. From Cockburn's use-case work it inherited the idea that user goals nest at different altitudes — summary, user-goal, sub-function — which is exactly what the map's vertical axis encodes. From Cockburn again it took the walking skeleton, and from the lean-startup movement, then ascendant, it absorbed the notion that the first release exists to produce evidence rather than revenue.

The problem it was invented to solve was an iatrogenic one: agile methods had cured the unread requirements document and induced a new disease. The flat backlog is an excellent queue and a terrible model. It answers "what next?" and cannot answer "what is the shape of this?" or "what is missing?" Patton's observation was that the shape had been thrown away not by accident but by the data structure, and that restoring a second dimension restored the ability to see gaps.

There is genuine disagreement about what follows from that, and the disagreement is not merely emphasis. Four positions are worth stating in the form of propositions each camp would and would not sign.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the formal treatment

The published version of the method has four steps — write the backbone, decompose into stories, order each column, draw release lines. Expert practice contains at least four more, and they are the ones that carry the value.

Choosing the mapped actor, and accepting that a map is per-actor. Raman's system touches a field technician, a billing operator, a consumer and a regulator. A single backbone containing all four produces rows that cannot be released, because half the row belongs to a person who is not present. Rudraksh drew three maps and aligned them on shared events — the moment a reading lands, the moment a bill is issued — which is the standard expert manoeuvre and the source of most of the difficulty described in section 5.

Deriving the backbone from observed behaviour rather than from the product's screens. Barve's team had a journey map from research done in June across thirty-one users; it contained a phase the product had no screen for, which users described as "checking whether I'm still on track," and which turned out to be where retention lived. A backbone read off the existing navigation would have omitted it.

Ordering each column by necessity rather than by value. The top card in a column is the crudest version of that step that still lets the user proceed. This is a different ordering principle from the one used in a ranked backlog, and mixing them silently is a common source of incoherent slices.

Naming the riskiest assumption before drawing the line. The map presents a menu of feasible releases; it does not choose among them. The choice requires a belief about uncertainty that comes from outside the map. Teams that skip this step do not avoid making the choice; they make it implicitly, usually by cutting evenly, which silently asserts that all columns are equally uncertain.

The formal treatment

Story mapping is usually taught without mathematics, which is a pity, because the release-line decision has an exact and illuminating statement. Let the map have n activities indexed by j. Within activity j there are candidate implementations ordered from crudest to richest, with costs cj1 < cj2 < …. A release is a choice of one implementation level per activity. Let C be capacity. Then:

The minimum feasible skeleton costs S = Σj cj1 — the sum of the cheapest card in every column. If S > C, no end-to-end release exists inside the deadline and the correct action is to narrow the population, not the journey. If S ≤ C, the quantity C − S is slack, and the entire real decision is how to spend it. Note what this reframing does: it turns a ranking problem over 612 items into a coverage-constrained allocation problem over nine columns. That is a categorically easier problem for a human to reason about, and it is the deepest thing the technique offers.

With S = 620 and slack of 2,440 days, Raman's problem is no longer "what shall we cut." It is "what shall we buy with 2,440 engineer-days," which admits a decision rule. For each candidate thickening, estimate the probability p that the underlying assumption is wrong and the loss L if that is discovered at the end of the programme rather than now. The expected value of learning early is approximately p × L; the cost is days × the fully loaded daily rate, which at Rudraksh was ₹18,000. Buy in descending order of ratio.

The arithmetic should not be mistaken for precision. Both p and L are guesses, and the ordering is robust only when the ratios differ by an order of magnitude, as rows one and four do here. What the calculation actually buys is a conversation in which a delivery head has to say out loud that he thinks there is a 15% chance the tariff assumption is wrong — and then to defend 120 days against that number. Teams that have never written the numbers down argue about the features instead, and the argument has no terminating condition.

4. When the technique applies, and when it is actively misleading

Four conditions can be stated as testable claims. Apply each to both protagonists.

Claim one: the product has a sequential journey that a single actor experiences as a sequence. True for Barve — a Rohanika Money user genuinely proceeds from naming a goal to funding it. Partly true for Raman: the consumer's journey is sequential, but the operator's day is a queue of unrelated exceptions, not a journey, and mapping it as one produces a fiction. Where the actor's experience is a queue rather than a path, the horizontal axis carries no information and the map degenerates into a categorised list — useful, but no longer a map.

Claim two: value is realised only at the end of the journey. Strongly true in both cases, which is why both needed the technique. Where it is false — a reference product, a documentation site, an analytics dashboard where each chart is independently valuable — slicing vertically is unnecessary and the flat ranked list is genuinely the better instrument. The most common misapplication of story mapping is to products where the user's tasks are independent.

Claim three: the crudest version of each step is materially cheaper than the good version. True in most software; false wherever a floor exists. Raman's column 9 has a regulatory floor; Barve's column 3, know-your-customer verification, has a larger one. An investment platform in India cannot onboard an investor with a crude identity check: the intermediary must complete a prescribed verification and file the record with the central KYC registry, and the thinnest defensible implementation of that step cost Barve 96 of his 242 skeleton days — 40% of the entire skeleton on one column out of six.

Claim four: you can observe what happens after the release. True for Barve, whose users are instrumented and numerous. Much weaker for Raman, whose "users" are 4 lakh electricity consumers she cannot survey and one utility client whose feedback arrives through a monthly governance meeting. When the feedback loop is slow and mediated, the value of a thin slice falls, because the learning it buys arrives too late to change the next slice. This is the single most under-appreciated boundary condition of the technique, and it explains why enterprise teams so often rationally choose thicker first releases than the literature recommends.

5. Hard edge cases

Two-sided markets. A marketplace has two backbones that must both walk or neither does. Rohanvi Bazaar, a Hyderabad platform matching school students to tutors, learned this at cost: its first skeleton served the student journey end to end and left tutors on a manual onboarding spreadsheet, which worked until 60 tutors became 600 and the spreadsheet became the constraint on student experience. The standard expert move is to draw both maps, align them on the transaction event, and then decide explicitly which side the company will impersonate in release one — because a marketplace skeleton nearly always requires the company to act as the missing side, at its own cost and risk.

Regulated products. Floors, as above. The subtler effect is that in regulated domains "crude" and "non-compliant" are easy to confuse, and the confusion runs in both directions. Teams thin a step they were not permitted to thin; or, more often, they refuse to thin a step that was never regulated in the first place, because the compliance function was asked "can we?" rather than "what specifically is required?" The diagnostic is to require a citation: which rule, which clause, what exactly does it oblige.

Hardware plus software. Rudrakoot Devices, which builds prepaid water meters for housing societies, cannot iterate a column that has been injection-moulded. The expert adaptation is to split the backbone into a hardware-committed prefix and a software-flexible suffix, fix the release line for the prefix at the tooling date, and accept that the map has a vertical wall in it. Story mapping still helps, but the walking skeleton must walk on last year's hardware.

AI-native products. Where a column is implemented by a model rather than by deterministic code, the crudest version of the step is not cheaper in the usual way — it is cheap to build and expensive to trust. Rudraveena AI, which sells an automated first-response agent for consumer-support queues, found that the thin version of "draft a reply" took four days to build and eleven weeks to evaluate, because the cost had migrated from construction into evaluation. The practical consequence is that the estimate on such a card must include its evaluation harness, or the skeleton will walk into production and fall over in a way nobody can debug.

Organisational seams. This is where mature companies differ most sharply from what they say. In a single-team company a release line is a decision. In a company where columns 2 and 4 belong to a platform group with its own quarterly commitments, a release line is a negotiation, and the map's practical function shifts from planning to diplomacy: it is the only artefact on which a platform lead can see that his column is the one gating everyone else's evidence. What mature companies actually do — as distinct from the published process — is appoint a single accountable owner for the line and give that person the authority to pull a column forward across a team boundary. Where that authority does not exist, maps get drawn, admired and then quietly overridden by each team's own roadmap, and the release ships horizontally after all.

6. The nuances that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

Thin means crude and complete, never good and partial

The competent practitioner slices by reducing quality; the expert slices by reducing quality while holding completeness fixed. "An ops executive telephones the consumer" is thin and complete. "Self-service booking that works only in one postal code" is thin and partial, and it destroys the measurement: when 42% of users drop out you cannot tell whether they rejected the proposition or hit the hole. The tell-tale sign in the wild is a release whose success metric has to be reported "for eligible users only." The obvious reading — that a partial feature is a smaller feature — is wrong, because a partial feature does not reduce scope so much as it contaminates evidence.

Manual implementation is legitimate, but its economics never generalise

A step performed by a person satisfies the skeleton condition provided the user's experience of it is genuine. The expert's caveat is that a concierge step tests the demand but not the business, and the two are routinely conflated. Rohanika Money could have staffed KYC review manually; it would have learned that users complete it, and learned nothing about whether the unit economics survive at 40,000 accounts a month. The tell is a team celebrating a conversion rate achieved with an operating cost per transaction they have never calculated. Set the volume at which the manual step must be replaced, in writing, before the slice ships.

Narrative order is not build order, and confusing them is expensive

The backbone is the sequence the user lives, not the sequence the team builds. Raman's column 6 — collect payment — was started in week one, because the payment-rail integration had a six-week onboarding cycle with the bank. The recognisable symptom of the confusion is a plan in which the team spends the first third of the schedule polishing columns 1 and 2 "because they come first," and arrives at the integration with four weeks left.

Estimates on the thin cards are biased low in a specific, predictable way

The crude version of a step often must handle the same edge cases as the rich one. A payout of ₹4,700 and a payout of ₹4.7 lakh both clear the same bank verification even if the screen is ugly. Expert practice inflates thin-card estimates rather than deflating them, and sizes the first slice to leave slack rather than to consume the budget. A team whose skeleton consumes more than about half of capacity has, in practice, no skeleton.

The map's coverage constraint is what makes scoring methods usable, not what replaces them

The map answers "what must be present for this release to work?" It is silent on "which of two equally releasable slices is worth more?" Value-versus-effort, RICE and weighted scoring answer the second and are meaningless without the first: a story with an excellent RICE score that leaves column 5 empty is worth nothing, because the release containing it cannot ship. The recognisable error is a backlog where the top twenty items by score cannot be assembled into anything a user can complete. This is precisely the failure that the best teaching of this module is designed to expose — a deliberately noisy backlog, scored confidently, that turns out not to constitute a product.

A map is per-actor, and aligning maps is a harder skill than drawing one

Every column boundary asserts something about how one person experiences time. Change the person and the backbone changes entirely. The expert draws several maps and aligns them on shared events rather than merging them into one row; the competent practitioner draws one map of "the user" and then cannot explain why the release keeps leaving holes. The sign is a backbone in which two adjacent activities have different grammatical subjects.

Slack allocation, not slicing, is where the value actually is

Once the minimum feasible skeleton is computed, almost all remaining capacity is discretionary, and almost all teaching of the technique stops exactly there. An expert spends the slack deliberately — on the columns whose assumptions are weakest — and can state the expected information purchase for each allocation. The tell is whether a team can answer "what will release one tell you that you do not already know?" without describing features.

The technique disciplines execution; it cannot validate the proposition

A map assumes the journey is the right journey. If electricity consumers do not want a digital bill at all, Raman's map is a well-organised plan for building something unwanted, and every slice will walk competently in the wrong direction. The map sits downstream of customer journey mapping and downstream of the decision to build. Experts say this out loud when presenting a map, because the artefact's confident geometry invites the opposite inference.

Maps decay, and the decay is silent

A map is a representation of a plan, and plans change daily. Unless there is an explicit ritual for placing new stories into columns, the flat backlog quietly reasserts itself within about three sprints while the photograph of the sticky notes remains on the wiki as evidence that the team "does mapping." The diagnostic is to ask where a story written yesterday lives on the map. Hesitation is the answer.

A map with no empty-looking columns is usually an incomplete map

Real journeys contain steps that nobody has thought about — error recovery, the second attempt, the consumer who moves house mid-cycle. A backbone in which every column is comfortably populated generally reflects the team's existing intentions rather than the user's actual path. Experts deliberately hunt for the sparse column, because a sparse column is either a step nobody has planned for or a step that does not exist, and both findings are valuable.

7. How it differs across product types and company stages

In consumer products the backbone is short and observable and the hard work is vertical: there are dozens of defensible implementations of "see plan," and the map's value is in forcing the crudest. Feedback is fast and quantitative, which raises the return on thin slices and justifies more of them.

In B2B and enterprise the backbone is longer, spans several people inside the customer, and the feedback loop runs through a governance meeting rather than an analytics event. Thinness by crudeness is often unavailable, because an auditable process cannot be done crudely; thinness by population — one division, one tariff category, one laboratory — is the substitute. Raman's real lever was not a thinner column but 12,000 consumers in a single sub-division rather than 4 lakh across the state.

In platforms and marketplaces the structural fact is two backbones and a transaction event where they meet; the first release almost always requires the company to supply one side manually or on its own balance sheet.

In hardware the map has a wall at the tooling date, and the software columns must be planned around a physical commitment that cannot be re-sliced.

In AI products the cost of a thin card migrates from construction to evaluation, and any estimate omitting the evaluation harness is fiction.

By stage, the honest answer is that the technique changes less than people expect. What changes is its function. In a twenty-person company the map is drawn in an afternoon by everyone who will build it and its value is shared understanding; the artefact can be thrown away. In a two-thousand-person company the map crosses team boundaries and its value becomes the negotiation described in section 5; the artefact must survive, must have an owner, and must be reconciled with quarterly planning, which is a genuine cost and not a ceremony. Claims that early-stage companies "do not need" mapping are usually claims that a four-person team already holds the map in shared memory — which is true, and stops being true at about the tenth engineer.

8. Three worked examples

Rohanika Money: the mid-journey floor

Barve's skeleton came to 242 days against 507 of capacity: 14 for naming a goal, 26 for the plan, 96 for identity verification, 48 for funding, 18 for tracking, 40 for withdrawal. Forty per cent of the skeleton sat in a single column he could not compress, and it sat third of six, which meant no downstream assumption could be tested until it was paid for. His alternative was population narrowing: restrict release one to the 410,000 users who had already transacted and were therefore already verified, reducing column 3 from 96 days to 21 — a reuse of existing verification records rather than a new flow. The skeleton fell to 167 days, and the three downstream columns became observable in week five rather than week nine. The cost was that the release could say nothing about new-user acquisition, which Barve wrote into the plan as an explicit unanswered question rather than allowing it to be assumed.

Rudraksh Grid Systems: buying the right information

Raman's 620-day skeleton plus the first three rows of Table 3 came to 785 days, leaving 2,275 for two subsequent slices. She ran the skeleton against one sub-division of 12,000 consumers with a live bill cycle in December — real meters, real money, real regulatory report — and found in the second week what Table 3 had priced at a 29:1 ratio: 22% of consumer records in the legacy master had a mismatch between the meter serial and the consumer account. Discovered in December that was a data-remediation project costing 180 days. Discovered in March it would have been the whole contract.

Rohitak Insure Cloud: where it failed, and what recovery looked like

Rohitak Insure Cloud, a health-insurance claims platform in Gurugram, mapped the member's claim journey competently in early 2024 and shipped a skeleton in eleven weeks: notify, submit documents, adjudicate, approve, pay. The failure was in column 3. The team implemented adjudication "thinly" by supporting only cashless claims at network hospitals in one city — thin and partial rather than thin and crude. Forty-two per cent of members who began a claim never completed one, and the team spent five weeks arguing about whether this reflected a product problem or the eligibility gap, because the instrumentation could not distinguish them. The recovery, in August, was to re-cut on the other axis: keep every claim type, adjudicate all of them manually with four trained assessors at roughly ₹4.6 lakh a month, and restrict by member population — one corporate account of 9,400 lives — rather than by claim type. Completion was then measurable at 71%, and the manual assessors produced a rule set that became the automation specification. The lesson Rohitak's head of product drew afterwards was blunt: when you must narrow, narrow the people, not the path.

9. Failure modes and their early warnings

The layer-cake release. Early sign: a week-eight status report claiming 60% completion with nothing a user can do. Diagnostic question: what can a named user accomplish end to end today? If the answer needs the word "once," the slice is horizontal. Cost of catching it late: the entire budget, since a layered plan produces its first evidence only at the end.

The sitemap posing as a backbone. Early sign: activities named Home, Search, Account. Diagnostic: read the backbone aloud with "the consumer" as the subject of each box; "the consumer Account" is audibly not a sentence. Cost late: a plan organised around navigation that omits the phases users actually feel, which are where retention lives.

The line drawn by capacity rather than by risk. Early sign: the first release contains exactly the number of stories that fits the quarter, and nobody can say what it will teach. Diagnostic: what result would change the plan for release two? Silence means the slice was chosen arithmetically. Cost late: a full cycle spent confirming what was already believed.

Thin-and-partial instead of thin-and-crude. Early sign: the success metric is qualified by eligibility. Diagnostic: can the drop-off be attributed? Cost late: Rohitak's five weeks of unresolvable argument, plus the risk that the wrong conclusion is drawn confidently.

The dead map. Early sign: the map lives in a photograph and the work lives in a tracker. Diagnostic: where does yesterday's new story sit? Cost late: the reappearance of every pathology the map was drawn to prevent, now with the reassuring appearance of process.

Seam collapse. Early sign: one team's columns slip and the others ship anyway. Diagnostic: compute each team's share of the skeleton and compare it with that team's objectives. Cost late: a release that is complete in two-thirds of the journey, which is to say not complete.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Is the skeleton for technical or commercial de-risking? The architectural position, steelmanned: integration failures are the ones that cannot be recovered late, because they are structural rather than incremental; a skeleton that exercises every real integration on day one converts the most dangerous class of unknown into a known, and the evidence for this is the long history of programmes that discovered in month five that two systems could not reconcile. The commercial position, steelmanned: technical risk is usually estimable by experienced engineers while demand risk is not, so the scarce resource — an early release — should be spent where estimation fails, and the evidence is the larger history of technically flawless products nobody wanted. The first would be wrong if integrations in a given stack had become genuinely routine; the second would be wrong if the demand question had already been answered by an existing product line, which in Raman's contracted enterprise case it largely had. Notice that the two positions generate different first releases from the same map, and that neither is generically correct.

Journey spine or opportunity spine? The discovery school argues that the current journey encodes yesterday's solution, so organising work along it structurally prevents reconceiving the problem; organise by customer opportunity instead. Steelmanned, this is strong: Rohanika Money's backbone assumes goal-based investing is delivered through a plan and instalments, and a map cannot question that. The mapping school replies that the opportunity tree is the right instrument for choosing what to build and the wrong instrument for slicing what has been chosen, because opportunities do not have a completeness constraint and releases do. The honest position is that these are instruments for different moments, but practitioners who hold one strongly do genuinely under-use the other, and the disagreement about sequencing is real.

Does continuous delivery make release planning obsolete? The flow school argues that with trunk-based development, feature flags and daily deploys, the batch is already one story and the "release" is a marketing event; maps solve a problem created by batching. Steelmanned with evidence from teams shipping forty times a day, this is serious. The counter is that flags decouple deployment from exposure but not from coherence: a user still cannot complete a journey whose fourth step is dark, so somebody still has to know which set of flags constitutes a walkable path. That knowledge is a map, whether or not it is drawn.

Is concierge implementation honest? One camp holds that a manual step is the purest form of thinness, since the user's experience is real and only the mechanism is deferred. The other holds that it systematically flatters the product, because the manual step is executed by motivated staff with unlimited attention, producing quality the automated version will never match, and because it tests demand while concealing economics. Both are right about different things, and the disagreement is unresolved because it turns on an empirical question — how much of measured conversion is attributable to the manual step's quality — that almost nobody instruments.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this behaves differently in three observable ways. First, when a stakeholder asks for a feature, they respond with a location rather than a verdict: which column, above or below which card. The request is thereby converted from a yes-or-no into a trade, and the trade is visible. Second, when a deadline compresses, they do not remove items from the bottom of a list; they raise a line across a journey and then argue about which two columns must stay thick, and they can state the reason in terms of uncertainty rather than importance. Third, and most diagnostically, they can say before a release ships what number will tell them whether the assumption held and what they will do at each side of it — Barve's threshold was a 55% plan-to-first-instalment conversion, below which the proposition would be reconsidered rather than iterated.

The person who has merely studied the technique draws a beautiful map, photographs it, and then ranks the backlog exactly as they would have done before.

12. What each protagonist decided

On 22 September, Raman committed to a skeleton of 785 engineer-days covering all nine columns for a single sub-division of 12,000 consumers, with a live December bill cycle, real payment collection and a real regulatory report filed on the prescribed format. Columns 2 and 4 — the platform group's 236 days — were escalated to the delivery head and given a fixed internal date of 14 November, with Raman named as owner of the release line across all three teams. The time-of-day tariff work, 120 days at an information ratio of 0.17, was deferred to slice two without apology.

On 26 September, Barve narrowed by population rather than by path: goal-based investing would launch on 1 December to already-verified users only, a 167-day skeleton, with the new-user verification flow explicitly listed in the plan as an unanswered question rather than a deferred feature — a distinction he insisted on in writing, because deferred features get forgotten and unanswered questions get asked.

Three questions for discussion. First: Raman's information ratios rest on probabilities she invented; does writing down a number she cannot defend improve the decision or merely decorate it, and what would you require before accepting such a table in a steering meeting? Second: Barve's narrowing preserves measurement but excludes precisely the users the proposition was designed to attract — under what conditions is evidence from an unrepresentative population worth more than no evidence at all? Third: if the flow school is right that continuous delivery dissolves release planning, what exactly replaces the coverage constraint, and who holds it?

13. Going deeper

Customer journey mapping is the direct upstream dependency: a backbone drawn without research is drawn on assumption, and the phases users feel but have no screen for — Barve's "am I still on track" — only appear from interview data. Learn it first if your backbones keep turning into sitemaps.

Value vs effort gives you the simplest way to choose between two slices that both walk, and introduces the habit of putting effort on an axis rather than in a footnote. It is the smallest useful complement to the coverage constraint.

RICE scoring adds reach and confidence to that comparison and is the standard vocabulary in most product organisations — which is exactly why it is dangerous when learned as vocabulary. Its output is only meaningful over items that can actually ship together, which is what a map establishes.

The Kano model explains why some thin cards are acceptable to users and others are not: a crude implementation of a basic expectation causes dissatisfaction out of proportion to its size, which is the missing theory behind the notion of a column floor.

Weighted scoring and WSJF extend prioritisation to multiple stakeholder criteria and to cost of delay, and cost of delay is the formal cousin of the L term in Table 3 — worth learning if you want the information-purchase argument on firmer ground.

Buy-a-feature is the cheapest way to elicit relative preference from real customers or from internal stakeholders under a budget constraint, and it pairs naturally with a map: give people the slack days as currency and watch which columns they thicken.

Prioritising under constraints generalises everything above to the situation both protagonists were actually in — fixed date, fixed team, negotiable scope — and is the module's synthesis topic. Take it once the coverage constraint feels automatic rather than clever.
